patient.chief_complaint: Prolonged unresponsiveness, rhythmic extremity movements — EEG team disagrees whether this is NCSE or psychogenic non-epileptic status
patient.history_present_illness: A 38-year-old Hispanic female nurse was brought to the emergency department by her colleague after prolonged unresponsive episodes at their hospital unit. The patient had been at work when she suddenly became unresponsive and collapsed. Her colleague reported that she appeared to have rhythmic shaking of both arms for several minutes, then appeared to 'wake up' briefly, then became unresponsive again with more subtle rhythmic movements of the legs. Total duration of apparent seizure-like activity was over 30 minutes before EMS arrived. She has a known diagnosis of epilepsy diagnosed 8 years ago with generalized tonic-clonic seizures, now well-controlled on lamotrigine for the past 3 years without a breakthrough seizure. The colleague noted she had been under extreme stress recently — her mother was hospitalized with cancer last week, and she had been working 12-hour night shifts. The colleague is also aware the patient has a history of psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES), diagnosed 2 years ago after video-EEG monitoring, and has been in therapy. The patient is known to have both true epilepsy and PNES — a common and diagnostically challenging combination. On EMS arrival, she was unresponsive with eyes closed, making occasional moaning sounds. On ED arrival, 35 minutes after onset, she continues with intermittent bilateral arm trembling with eyes closed. She is not responding to commands. EMG artifact and motion artifact make initial EEG interpretation extremely challenging. Lamotrigine level drawn on arrival.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Appears unresponsive with eyes closed. Intermittent moaning. When examiner attempts to open eyelids, patient actively closes eyes — 'active eye closure' sign. Occasional purposeful-appearing arm movements inconsistent with epileptic activity.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, equal and reactive. No oculomotor palsy. No corneal reflex abnormality. Eyes actively close when opened by examiner — high-specificity PNES feature.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral rhythmic arm trembling that waxes and wanes. Movements irregular in amplitude and frequency. No sustained tonic posturing. No Jacksonian march.
neurological_exam.sensory: Appears not to respond to noxious stimuli, but withdrawal inconsistent with true unconsciousness.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ throughout. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Babinski.
neurological_exam.additional: Semiological features: eyes closed throughout, active eye closure when opened, waxing-waning intensity of movements, pelvic thrusting noted intermittently, head turning side to side — all high-specificity PNES features. No post-ictal confusion period after movements resolve — incompatible with epileptic seizure.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL EEG. Normal 9-10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm bilaterally; no focal slowing; no epileptiform discharges; no electrographic seizures recorded. The posterior dominant rhythm was persistently present during clinical shaking episodes recorded on this study. Extensive motion/EMG artifact during clinical events significantly limits interpretation and cannot be excluded as a source of false-negative results. Video-EEG with improved artifact control is recommended for definitive characterization of events. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: This is a NORMAL EEG. Normal 9-10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm was persistently present during all 3 clinical events captured on simultaneous video-EEG. results.title: Treatment of psychogenic nonepileptic seizures
results.key_finding: Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is the only evidence-based treatment for PNES with Level A recommendation. Communicating diagnosis clearly and compassionately is essential. Benzodiazepine use for presumed SE in PNES patients is a common harmful error — may reinforce behavior, cause respiratory depression, and delay appropriate psychiatric treatment. Video-EEG is the gold standard diagnostic test.

output.summary: Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) has Level A evidence for treatment of psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) and is the recommended first-line treatment. Video-EEG is the diagnostic gold standard for PNES; a normal EEG during captured clinical events supports the diagnosis. Unnecessary escalation of antiseizure medications in confirmed PNES is associated with harm without benefit. Psychogenic non-epileptic status is managed with non-pharmacological de-escalation in the absence of confirmed electrographic seizure activity. CBT has been associated with a 50-70% reduction in event frequency in published trials.

results.title: Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures in patients with comorbid epilepsy
results.key_finding: 20-40% of PNES patients have coexisting epilepsy. Lamotrigine appropriate for JME. PNES events must be distinguished from epileptic events using video-EEG. Key distinguishing features of PNES: eyes closed during events, active eye-closure, normal EEG during events, normal prolactin post-event, waxing-waning symptom intensity, pelvic thrusting, side-to-side head shaking.

output.summary: Coexisting PNES and epilepsy is reported in 20-40% of PNES patients; the combination is diagnostically challenging. Antiseizure medications are appropriate for treating comorbid epilepsy but do not benefit PNES events. Key EEG and semiological features that distinguish PNES from epileptic seizures include: normal EEG during captured events, preserved posterior dominant rhythm, eyes-closed semiology with active resistance to eye opening, waxing-waning event intensity, normal post-ictal prolactin, and normal lactate/CK. Video-EEG is the diagnostic gold standard for definitive event characterization.
